title: Safe Foraging
summary: How to identify edible wild plants and perform the Universal Edibility Test.

sections.heading: Step 1 — Know Poisonous Plant Indicators
sections.body: Avoid wild plants that exhibit any of these traits unless positively identified as edible: milky or colored sap; red/white/yellow berries; three-leaf growth patterns (like poison ivy); shiny or fuzzy leaves; umbrella-shaped flowers (like deadly hemlock); or an almond-like scent (indicating cyanide).
sections.warning: Never eat wild mushrooms unless you are an expert mycologist. Mistakes are often fatal.
sections.image_description: Illustration of plant with milky white sap and clusters of white berries

sections.heading: Step 2 — Identify Easy and Safe Wild Plants
sections.body: Focus on easily recognizable, widely distributed plants. Examples include: Dandelions (all parts edible); Cattails (roots and inner stalks edible); Clover (leaves can be eaten raw or boiled); and Pine needles (steeped in hot water to make Vitamin-C rich tea).
sections.warning: Make sure you harvest plants far away from busy roads, industrial sites, or sprayed agricultural fields.
sections.image_description: Sketches of dandelion flower, clover, and cattail reed

sections.heading: Step 3 — Perform the Universal Edibility Test
sections.body: If you must eat an unknown plant, test one part (leaf, root, or stem) at a time: 1. Touch to skin for 15 mins (check for rash). 2. Hold a small cooked portion on lips for 3 mins. 3. Place on tongue for 15 mins without swallowing. 4. Chew for 15 mins. 5. If no burning/bitterness, swallow. Wait 8 hours. If no stomach issues, the tested part is relatively safe.
sections.warning: Only perform this test in extreme survival emergencies. Never rush the process.
sections.image_description: Sequence showing skin test, lip test, tongue test, and wait time

sections.heading: Step 4 — Process Acorns and Seeds
sections.body: Acorns are a high-calorie wild food source but contain bitter, toxic tannic acid. Crush the shelled acorns and leach the tannins by boiling them in multiple changes of water until the water runs clear. Roast or grind into flour once leached.
sections.warning: Raw acorns can cause severe stomach cramps and kidney damage.
sections.image_description: Crushed acorns boiling in a pot with brown water being drained

when_to_use: When you have run out of packaged rations and need to supplement calories in a wilderness survival scenario.
do_not: Eat unknown plants that smell like bitter almonds
Skip the waiting period during the edibility test
Eat raw acorns or raw wild tubers
sources: Peterson Field Guide to Edible Wild Plants
